segments.text: Πολὺ ὕστερον ὁ Γρύλλος πρὸς Ὀλυμπίαν θεῖ, ὁ δὲ πατὴρ αὐτὸν καλεῖ.
«Ἀνάμενε· οὐ θηράσομεν νῦν,» λέγει ὁ Ξενοφῶν· «τὴν μητέρα οὐ δεῖ λείπειν.»

segments.text: Ἡ δὲ Φιλησία τὴν χεῖρα τοῦ Διοδώρου λαμβάνει· πολὺς γὰρ ὄχλος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ.

segments.speaker: char-diodoros

grammar.title: Φοβοῦμαι · δέδοικα
grammar.rule: φοβοῦμαι μή … · δέδοικα μὴ φύγῃ · φοβοῦμαι μὴ οὐ βοηθήσῃ

tables.caption: μή · μὴ οὐ
rows: I fear that Diodorus may get lost.
I fear that he may take the roof off.
I fear that he may see us … may escape.
I fear that he may not help.
I am afraid to go near.

grammar.note_en:
A fear clause states an event someone dreads. A clause is a group of words built around a verb; a dependent clause needs another clause to complete its sense. In «φοβοῦμαι μὴ ὁ Διόδωρος ἐν τῷ ὄχλῳ ἀπόληται» (s004), “I fear that Diodorus may get lost in the crowd,” φοβοῦμαι gives the fear, and everything from μή onward gives the feared event. Philesia does not say that Diodorus is already lost. Her fear makes her take his hand.

After a verb of fearing, μή introduces the possibility to be avoided. Here it does not mean that the following event is negative. «Δέδοικα μὴ φύγῃ» (s023) means “I fear that he may escape,” not “I fear that he may not escape.” To fear a failure to act, Greek adds οὐ: «φοβοῦμαι μὴ οὐ βοηθήσῃ» (s027), “I fear that he may not help.” Read μή as the link to the fear, then οὐ as the negative belonging to helping. Xenophon wants the official to help; he fears the opposite.

The dependent verbs are subjunctive. A mood indicates how an action is presented: here as a feared possibility rather than an asserted fact. You already know the long vowels of the subjunctive. The aorist forms present each event as a whole; they do not put it in the past. ἀπόληται, “may get lost,” uses the stem ἀπ-ολ- and a middle ending. ἀφέλῃ, “may take away,” uses ἀφ-ελ-; ἴδῃ, “may see,” uses ἰδ-; φύγῃ, “may escape,” uses φυγ-. Recognise the stem before the ending. The indicative augment belongs to past indicative forms and is absent here.

Every fear clause in this chapter follows a present verb in direct speech. This is primary sequence: the time and standpoint of the main verb support the subjunctive in its dependent clause. δέδοικα is a special lexicalised perfect: a form historically built as a perfect but used with the present meaning “I fear.” Learn it as a word here, without constructing a new perfect paradigm. Past narration outside the quotation does not change the speaker’s present fear.

Compare «φοβοῦμαι ἐγγὺς ἰέναι» (s016), “I am afraid to go near.” The infinitive ἰέναι names the action Diodorus himself is afraid to attempt. A fear clause can instead have its own subject: in «δέδοικα μὴ ὁ θεὸς ἀναστὰς τὴν στέγην ἀφέλῃ» (s011), “I fear that the god, rising, may take the roof off,” Diodorus fears and the god rises and acts. ἀναστάς is a participle, a verb form describing the subject alongside the main action. It adds one compact action within the fear clause, without introducing a condition.

parergon.title: Καίτοι
parergon.body_en: καίτοι introduces a reservation against what has just been said: “and yet.” Xenophon doubts the official will help him; Philesia answers «καίτοι τὸν νόμον φυλάττει» (s028), “and yet he upholds the law.” She counters his worry with a reason to seek help. Later the official uses καίτοι against the seller’s claim (s045). The particle does not change the mood of a verb or introduce a fear clause. Look for the earlier claim that the following words challenge.

pair.sense_grc: ἀναιρεῖ: κάτω κεῖται, ὁ δὲ ἄνω φέρει

families.spelling_note: ἀπό- → ἀφ-αιρέω; ἀνά- → ἀν-αιρέω. Before the rough breathing of αἱρέω, ἀπό loses ο and π becomes φ; ἀνά loses its final α. Aorists in this reading use ἑλ-: ἀφείλοντο (past indicative, with augment), ἀφέλῃ (subjunctive, without augment). The pickup uses the present ἀναιρεῖ. ἀναιρέω can elsewhere mean kill or destroy; here the visible movement fixes the literal sense.
